title: Epilogue, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Siberia. On the banks of a wide, solitary river stands a town, one of Russia's administrative centers. In the town there is a fortress, and in the fortress there is a prison. In the prison, the second-class convict Rodion Raskolnikov has been confined for nine months. Almost a year and a half has passed since his crime.

His trial had proceeded without much difficulty. The prisoner adhered to his statement exactly, firmly, and clearly. He did not confuse or misrepresent the facts, did not soften them in his own favor, did not omit the smallest detail. He explained every aspect of the murder, including the secret of the pledge -- the piece of wood with a strip of metal -- found in the murdered woman's hand. He described in detail how he had taken her keys, what they looked like, the chest and its contents. He explained the mystery of Lizaveta's murder, described how Koch and then the student had knocked, and repeated every word they had said to each other. He told how he had run downstairs and heard Nikolay and Dmitri shouting, how he had hidden in the empty apartment and then gone home. He concluded by identifying the stone in the courtyard off Voznesensky Prospect, under which the purse and trinkets were found. The whole thing was perfectly clear. The lawyers and judges were particularly struck by the fact that he had hidden the trinkets and the purse under a stone without using them, and stranger still, that he couldn't even remember what the trinkets looked like or how many there were. The fact that he had never opened the purse and didn't even know how much was in it seemed incredible. The purse turned out to contain three hundred and seventeen rubles and sixty kopecks. Some of the larger notes on top had been damaged by moisture from lying so long under the stone. The court spent a long time trying to determine why the accused would lie about this one point when he had been truthful and straightforward about everything else. Some lawyers with more psychological insight ultimately conceded that it was possible he truly hadn't looked inside the purse and therefore didn't know what was in it when he hid it. But they immediately drew the conclusion that the crime could only have been committed in a state of temporary mental derangement -- homicidal mania without rational motive or pursuit of gain. This fit the latest fashionable theory of temporary insanity, which was increasingly applied in criminal cases. Moreover, Raskolnikov's depressive condition was confirmed by many witnesses -- Dr. Zossimov, his former classmates, his landlady, and her servant. All of this strongly supported the conclusion that Raskolnikov was not an ordinary murderer and thief, but that something else was at work.

To the intense annoyance of those who held this view, the criminal made almost no effort to defend himself. When asked the decisive question of what had driven him to murder and robbery, he answered with the bluntest frankness that the cause was his wretched circumstances, his poverty and helplessness, and his desire to secure his first steps in life with the three thousand rubles he had expected to find. He had been driven to murder by his shallow and cowardly nature, made worse by deprivation and failure. When asked what had led him to confess, he answered that it was sincere repentance. All of this was almost crudely blunt.

The sentence, however, was more lenient than might have been expected, partly because the criminal had not tried to justify himself but had rather seemed eager to exaggerate his guilt. All the strange and peculiar circumstances of the case were taken into account. There could be no doubt about the criminal's abnormal and poverty-stricken condition at the time. The fact that he had made no use of what he'd stolen was attributed partly to the onset of remorse, partly to his disturbed mental state during the crime. The incidental murder of Lizaveta actually supported the latter theory: a man commits two murders and then forgets that the door is open! Finally, his confession -- coming at the very moment when the case had been hopelessly muddled by Nikolay's false testimony, and when there were no proofs or even suspicions against the real criminal (Porfiry Petrovitch fully kept his word) -- all this did much to soften the sentence. Other circumstances also came to light unexpectedly in the prisoner's favor. Razumihin somehow discovered and proved that while at the university, Raskolnikov had helped support a sick fellow student for six months and, after that student died, had cared for his decrepit old father, eventually placing him in a hospital and paying for his funeral. Raskolnikov's landlady also testified that in their previous lodgings, Raskolnikov had rescued two small children from a burning building and been injured in the process. This was investigated and well confirmed by multiple witnesses. These facts made a favorable impression.
In the end, the criminal was sentenced -- in consideration of extenuating circumstances -- to penal servitude in the second class for a term of only eight years.

At the very start of the trial, Raskolnikov's mother fell ill. Dounia and Razumihin managed to get her out of Petersburg for the duration. Razumihin chose a town on the railway not far from the capital, so he could follow every step of the trial while also seeing Avdotya Romanovna as often as possible. Pulcheria Alexandrovna's illness was a strange nervous condition accompanied by a partial derangement of her mind.

When Dounia returned from her last meeting with her brother, she found their mother already ill, feverish and delirious. That evening she and Razumihin agreed on what they would tell her about Raskolnikov, concocting a complete story about his having to travel to a distant part of Russia on a business assignment that would eventually bring him money and recognition.

But they were struck by the fact that Pulcheria Alexandrovna never questioned them about it -- not then, not later. On the contrary, she had her own version of her son's sudden departure. She told them through tears how he had come to say goodbye, hinting that she alone knew many mysterious and important things, and that Rodya had many powerful enemies who made it necessary for him to go into hiding. As for his future career, she had no doubt it would be brilliant. His article and his obvious literary talent proved it. She read the article constantly, sometimes read it aloud, and practically took it to bed with her -- yet she hardly ever asked where Rodya actually was, even though the others obviously avoided the subject, which should have been enough to arouse her suspicions.

Eventually they grew frightened by Pulcheria Alexandrovna's strange silence on certain topics. She did not, for instance, complain about not receiving letters from him, though in previous years she had lived for nothing else but the hope of his letters. This alarmed Dounia greatly; she began to suspect that their mother sensed something terrible about her son's fate and was afraid to ask, for fear of learning something even worse. In any case, Dounia could see clearly that her mother was not in full possession of her faculties.

Once or twice, however, Pulcheria Alexandrovna steered the conversation in a direction that made it impossible to respond without mentioning where Rodya was, and when she received evasive, suspicious answers, she fell into a gloomy silence that lasted a long time. Dounia finally realized that it was pointless to try to deceive her and concluded that it was better to remain absolutely silent on certain subjects. But it became increasingly obvious that the poor mother suspected something terrible. Dounia remembered that her brother had mentioned their mother overhearing her talk in her sleep the night after the meeting with Svidrigailov, before the day of the confession. Had she understood something from that? Sometimes days and weeks of somber silence and tears would give way to a burst of hysterical excitement, and she would begin talking almost nonstop about her son, about her hopes for his future. Her fantasies were sometimes very strange. They humored her and pretended to agree -- she probably saw through their pretense -- but she kept talking.

Five months after Raskolnikov's confession, he was sentenced. Razumihin and Sonia visited him in prison as often as possible. At last the moment of separation arrived. Dounia swore to her brother that the separation would not be forever; Razumihin said the same. In his youthful fervor, Razumihin had firmly resolved to lay the foundations of a secure livelihood over the next three or four years, save up a certain sum, and emigrate to Siberia -- a land rich in natural resources and in need of workers, enterprising people, and capital. There they would settle in the town where Rodya was, and together they would begin a new life. They all wept at parting.

In the days before his departure, Raskolnikov had been very distracted. He asked often about his mother and was constantly worried about her. He fretted so much that Dounia became alarmed. When he learned of his mother's illness, he grew very somber. He was particularly reserved with Sonia throughout this time. With the help of the money Svidrigailov had left her, Sonia had long since made arrangements to follow the convoy of prisoners being sent to Siberia. Not a word was exchanged between Raskolnikov and her on the subject, but both knew that was how it would be. At the final farewell, he smiled strangely at his sister and Razumihin's passionate plans for their happy future together when he got out of prison. He predicted that their mother's illness would soon prove fatal. Then he and Sonia set off.

Two months later, Dounia married Razumihin. It was a quiet, sorrowful wedding. Porfiry Petrovitch and Zossimov were among those invited. Throughout this whole period, Razumihin wore an air of resolute determination. Dounia had complete faith in his plans, and indeed she could not help believing in him -- he showed a remarkable strength of will. Among other things, he resumed attending university lectures to finish his degree. They were constantly making plans for the future; both counted on settling in Siberia within five years at most. Until then, they placed their hopes on Sonia.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was delighted to bless Dounia's marriage to Razumihin, but after the wedding she grew even more melancholy and anxious. To cheer her, Razumihin told her how Raskolnikov had looked after the sick student and his old father, and how he had been burned rescuing two children from a fire. These two stories excited the disordered imagination of Pulcheria Alexandrovna almost to ecstasy. She talked about them incessantly, even striking up conversations with strangers in the street, though Dounia always accompanied her. In carriages and shops, wherever she could find a listener, she would launch into the story of her son, his article, his care for the student, his injuries from the fire. Dounia didn't know how to restrain her. Apart from the danger of her morbid excitement, there was the risk that someone might recall Raskolnikov's name and mention the recent trial. Pulcheria Alexandrovna managed to find the address of the mother of the two children he had saved and insisted on going to see her.

At last her agitation reached an extreme. She would sometimes burst into tears for no reason and was often ill and feverishly delirious. One morning she declared that by her reckoning, Rodya ought to be home soon -- she remembered that when he said goodbye, he had said to expect him back in nine months. She began preparing for his arrival, tidying up her room, cleaning the furniture, hanging new curtains. Dounia was worried but said nothing and helped. After an exhausting day of joyful daydreams and tears, Pulcheria Alexandrovna fell ill that night. By morning she was feverish and delirious. It was brain fever. She died within two weeks. In her delirium she let slip words that showed she had understood far more about her son's terrible fate than anyone had supposed.

For a long time Raskolnikov did not know of his mother's death, though regular correspondence had been maintained from the time he reached Siberia. The letters were carried on through Sonia, who wrote monthly to the Razumihins and received a reply with unfailing regularity. At first they found Sonia's letters dry and unsatisfying, but eventually they realized that nothing better was possible, for from these letters they received a complete picture of their unfortunate brother's life as a convict. Sonia's letters were filled with the most matter-of-fact detail, the simplest and clearest descriptions of Raskolnikov's surroundings. There was no word of her own hopes, no speculation about the future, no exploration of her feelings. Instead of any attempt to interpret his state of mind or inner life, she gave the plain facts -- his own words, an exact account of his health, what he asked for during their visits, what errands he gave her. All of it was reported with extraordinary precision. The picture of their unhappy brother emerged at last with great clarity. There could be no mistake, because nothing was given but facts.

But Dounia and her husband could draw little comfort from the news, especially at first. Sonia wrote that he was constantly sullen and barely willing to talk; that he showed scarcely any interest in the news from their letters; that he sometimes asked about his mother, and when she finally told him of her death -- seeing that he had already guessed the truth -- she was surprised to find he did not seem greatly affected, at least not outwardly. She reported that although he seemed entirely wrapped up in himself and had, as it were, shut himself off from everyone, he took a very direct and simple view of his new life. He understood his position, expected nothing better for the time being, harbored no ill-founded hopes (so common among prisoners), and seemed almost unsurprised by his surroundings, so different from anything he had known. She wrote that his health was satisfactory; he did his work without shirking or seeking to do more; he was almost indifferent about food, though it was so bad -- except on Sundays and holidays -- that he had eventually been glad to accept money from Sonia for tea every day. He begged her not to fuss about anything else, insisting that all this attention only annoyed him. Sonia added that in prison he shared quarters with the other inmates; she hadn't seen the inside of their barracks but gathered they were crowded, wretched, and unhealthy. He slept on a plank bed with a rug beneath him and refused any better arrangement -- not from any plan or principle, but simply from indifference and inattention.

Sonia wrote simply that at first he had shown no interest in her visits, had been almost angry with her for coming, reluctant to talk, and rude. But in time these visits became a habit and almost a necessity for him, so that he was genuinely upset when she fell ill for several days and couldn't come. She usually saw him on holidays at the prison gates or in the guardroom, where he was brought for a few minutes. On workdays she went to see him at his labor -- either at the workshops, the brick kilns, or the sheds on the banks of the Irtysh.

About herself, Sonia wrote that she had managed to make some acquaintances in the town and was doing sewing. Since there was barely a single dressmaker in the town, she had become practically indispensable in several households. She did not mention that through her efforts the authorities had taken an interest in Raskolnikov, or that his workload had been lightened, and so on.

At last the news came (Dounia had indeed noticed signs of alarm in the preceding letters) that he kept entirely to himself, that his fellow prisoners disliked him, that he went days without speaking, and that he was growing very pale. In her last letter, Sonia wrote that he had fallen seriously ill and had been taken to the prison hospital.
